sps-s2.name: Exercise Physiology: Energy Metabolism and Cardiorespiratory Adaptation
sps-s2.summary: Covers the three energy supply systems (ATP-PCr, glycolytic, and oxidative), maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max) and cardiac output based on the Fick equation, and the physiology of endurance adaptation at the lactate threshold (LT) and ventilatory threshold (VT).

sps-s3.name: Sports Biomechanics: Levers, Impulse, and Projectiles
sps-s3.summary: Covers the lever principle of the human skeletal muscles and torque equilibrium, ground reaction force (GRF) and the impulse-momentum theorem, moment of inertia and conservation of angular momentum, and the mechanics of optimal projection angles as a function of release height.

sps-s4.name: Motor Learning and Control: Information Processing, Schema Theory, and Practice Design
sps-s4.summary: Covers reaction-time information processing based on Hick's law, Schmidt's generalized motor program (GMP) and schema theory, blocked and random practice based on contextual interference, and the design of external focus and feedback (KR/KP).

sps-s5.name: Sport Psychology and Sociology, and Periodized Training Prescription
sps-s5.summary: Covers the inverted-U hypothesis of arousal and performance, the individual zone of optimal functioning (IZOF), Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy and the Ringelmann social loafing effect, the FITT-VP principle, and the design of microcycle, mesocycle, and macrocycle training.

sps-s6.name: Bachelor's Capstone: Integrated Sport Science Diagnosis and Training Design
sps-s6.summary: Students run a combined quantitative simulation of energy metabolism, ground reaction force, and angular momentum, then complete and evaluate a comprehensive prescription report covering biomechanical fault analysis, motor learning, and periodization for an elite athlete or a general adult.

sps-01.title: The Concept of Physical Activity and Health
explain: **Sport science** is the academic study of human physical activity and sport from several perspectives, including physiological, psychological, and social ones. This course is a **general education course that teaches general theory**. It is not guidance that tells a particular person how to exercise, assesses someone's physical condition, or addresses injuries or illnesses. If you have discomfort or concerns about your body, you should consult a professional such as a healthcare provider rather than this course. It also does not cover how to practice individual sports skills.

First, let us distinguish three words that are often used interchangeably. **Physical activity** is any behavior that uses muscles to move the body and expend energy. It includes walking, climbing stairs, and doing household chores. **Exercise** is a subset of physical activity that is planned and repeated in order to build or maintain physical fitness. **Sport** is physical activity that has rules and a competitive element. The three concepts nest like boxes of different sizes, but their boundaries are not sharply cut, and they can overlap.

explain.alt: Three boxes overlapping one another. The outer box is 'Physical activity', the middle box is 'Exercise', and the inner box is 'Sport', and each has a definition and an example written on it.
explain.caption: The starting point is to view them as physical activity ⊃ exercise ⊃ sport.

explain:
**Physical fitness** is the body's capacity needed to move. When discussed in relation to health, it is usually divided into the following five components.
- **Cardiorespiratory endurance**: the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen over a long period.
- **Muscular strength**: the amount of force a muscle can produce at one time.
- **Muscular endurance**: the ability of a muscle to repeat or sustain force over time.
- **Flexibility**: the range over which a joint can move.
- **Body composition**: the proportions of fat, muscle, bone, and other tissues that make up the body.

**Health** does not mean only the absence of disease. A widely used definition regards health as a state of physical, mental, and social well-being. Research has suggested that physical activity can be related to all three of these dimensions. However, saying that two things are related is different from saying that the same effect is guaranteed for everyone.

There is one more distinction to make. **Physical inactivity** and **sedentary time**, meaning long periods spent sitting, are different concepts. A person may exercise separately during the day and still spend most of the remaining time sitting, and the reverse is also possible. Research measures these two separately.

examples.title: Classifying everyday scenes
body: Consider a day in the life of a fictional person, Ha-yun. In the morning she walks quickly to the bus stop to catch a bus. At lunch, to build her fitness, she walks a route she has planned in advance. In the evening she plays a ringball game with friends from the neighborhood under agreed rules.

- Walking to the bus stop: it is not for fitness, so it is physical activity.
- Walking the planned route: it is planned and repeated, so it is exercise.
- Ringball game: it has rules and competition, so it is a sport.
The same walking can take different names depending on its purpose and planning. The reason for separating the concepts is to make clear what is being measured in research.

sps-02.title: Exercise and the Body
explain: The force that moves the body comes from **skeletal muscle**. Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and **contracts** when it receives nerve signals from the brain and spinal cord. Because muscle can only **pull** and cannot push, muscles that work in opposition form pairs, such as the muscles that bend and straighten the elbow.

The core explanation of what happens inside a muscle is the **sliding filament theory**. Within a muscle fiber, thin filaments of **actin** and thick filaments of **myosin** overlap. When a signal arrives, myosin pulls on actin so that the filaments slide past each other, and as a result the muscle fiber shortens and produces force. The actual process involves several factors, such as calcium, but for this course it is enough to remember this overall picture.

Muscle contractions are classified by how the length of the muscle changes.
- **Concentric contraction**: the muscle shortens while producing force.
- **Eccentric contraction**: the muscle lengthens while producing force. It is like lowering a heavy object slowly, where the muscle lengthens while resisting.
- **Isometric contraction**: force is produced but the length does not change. Pushing against an immovable wall is an example.

Muscle contraction requires energy. The energy currency that cells use directly is **ATP**. However, the amount of ATP stored in muscle is very small, and it runs out within a few seconds. For this reason the body keeps **resynthesizing** ATP. The ways of resynthesizing ATP are generally summarized into three **energy systems**.
- **Phosphagen system**: uses phosphocreatine stored in muscle. It does not require oxygen and is the fastest, but it cannot be sustained for long.
- **Glycolytic system**: breaks down glucose without using oxygen to produce ATP. It is relatively fast, but its duration is limited.
- **Oxidative system**: uses oxygen to break down carbohydrates and fats. It starts slowly but can be sustained for a long time.

explain.alt: A diagram of three bars showing the phosphagen, glycolytic, and oxidative systems in order of duration, with a description written beside each.
explain.caption: The three systems are arranged from short and intense to long and lower-intensity.

explain: The important point is that the three systems are **not switched on one at a time like switches**; they always work together. Only the share contributed by each system changes depending on the intensity and duration of the activity. It is also known that muscle fibers come in types that contract quickly and fatigue easily and types that are slow but can sustain effort for long periods, and the proportions differ from person to person.

Throughout the match, when he repeatedly runs back and forth across the court and his breathing rises and then settles, the glycolytic and oxidative systems both contribute a large share. Even so, the phosphagen system does not 'switch off.' Only its share changes.

sps-03.title: The Principles of Exercise Effects
explain: The body changes gradually in response to repeated stimuli. This is called **adaptation**. Exercise science uses many studies to explain what kinds of adaptation arise under which conditions. Below are some general principles that summarize this. **These are concepts for explanation and are not prescriptions telling anyone what to do.** Activity suited to an individual's health condition is a matter for experts to judge case by case.

The principle of **overload** holds that adaptation occurs only when a stimulus larger than the level the body normally experiences is applied. Simply repeating the same level of activity gives the body no reason to change. Here, 'larger' does not mean dangerously large in an unconditional sense; it means higher than usual, within the range the body can handle.

The principle of **progression** holds that adaptation continues only when the stimulus is raised gradually rather than suddenly. If a stimulus far outpaces the body's rate of adaptation, the result can be accumulated exhaustion rather than adaptation.

The principle of **specificity** holds that adaptation appears in line with the type of stimulus received. Activities that are light and continued for a long time tend to produce more adaptations related to the ability to supply oxygen over long periods, while activities that produce short, strong force tend to produce more adaptations related to force. For this reason, stimuli are designed differently depending on the ability being studied.

The principle of **reversibility** holds that when a stimulus stops, the adaptation gradually decreases. Finally, there are **individual differences**: even with the same stimulus, the size and speed of adaptation differ from person to person.

There is **recovery** between a stimulus and the adaptation. A stimulus first temporarily lowers the body's state. During rest, the body recovers to its original level, and a model that explains how, when conditions are right, it reaches a level slightly higher than before is called **supercompensation**. However, this figure is a conceptual model that simplifies the complex changes of the actual body.

explain.alt: A curve graph in which, after a stimulus, the body state drops below the baseline (fatigue), then rises above the baseline (supercompensation), and then returns to the baseline.

This result agrees with the principles of overload and progression. However, this hypothetical study does not lead to the conclusion 'so do this.' The principles are a framework that explains why change occurs, and the method suited to an individual is a separate question.

sps-04.title: Sport Psychology
explain: **Sport psychology** studies how people's thoughts, emotions, and motives affect their behavior and performance in exercise and competition. This is because results can differ depending on mental state even when physical ability is the same. This lesson is a conceptual introduction; it does not diagnose anyone's psychological state or explain how to manage it.

First is **motivation**. Motivation is the force that starts and sustains a behavior. **Intrinsic motivation** is engaging in an activity because it is enjoyable or meaningful in itself, while **extrinsic motivation** is engaging in it for reasons outside the activity, such as rewards, recognition, or pressure. Self-determination theory explains that motivation lasts longer when people feel they are choosing for themselves (autonomy), feel capable (competence), and feel connected to others (relatedness).

**Goal setting** is another important topic. Research suggests that specific, challenging but achievable goals are more readily linked to performance than vague goals such as 'do your best.' Also, people who judge success by whether they have mastered the **task** and people who judge it by **winning relative to others** may respond to failure in different ways.

Next are **arousal and anxiety**. **Arousal** is the degree to which the body and mind are awake and tense, and **anxiety** can be viewed as having a cognitive part, such as worry, and a physical part, such as a pounding heart. An older model that explains the relationship between arousal and performance is the **inverted-U hypothesis**. It holds that when arousal is too low, focus is loose and performance is low; when arousal is too high, tension lowers performance; and performance is highest at a moderate level.

explain.alt: An upside-down U-shaped curve. The horizontal axis is arousal level and the vertical axis is performance, with the peak at a moderate level.
explain.caption: The shape of the inverted-U hypothesis

explain: However, the hypothesis is also criticized for being too simple. Some argue that the best level of arousal depends on the nature of the task and on the person, and that the cognitive and physical parts of anxiety act differently. Therefore, it is appropriate to read this figure as **a starting-point model**.

We can explain that Seo-jun is driven mainly by intrinsic motivation and Min-a by extrinsic motivation. However, this is only an explanatory framework, and both kinds of motivation can be present in one person at the same time.

If, just before an important game, Seo-jun is so relaxed that he feels drowsy, we could say he is toward the left side of the inverted-U curve; if his hands shake from tension, he is toward the right side.

sps-05.title: Game Rules and Strategy
explain: Sport competition is shaped by **rules**. Rules do three things. First, they ensure **fairness**, so that competitors compete under the same conditions. Second, they ensure **safety** and protect athletes' bodies. Third, they govern **flow and identity**, keeping the game going and defining the character of the sport. Even with the same ball, different rules make a completely different sport.

This lesson uses a **fictional sport, 'ringball,'** created for explanation rather than a real sport. Its rules are as follows.
- A team has four players, and two teams compete on the court.
- The ball may be handled only with the hands. A player holding the ball may move up to three steps and must pass or shoot within five seconds.
- A shot can be taken **only by a player inside the scoring zone**. If the ball goes through the ring, it is worth two points.

explain.alt: A ringball court diagram with a scoring zone and a ring at each end, with four home-team players and four away-team players scattered across the court.
explain.caption: The ringball court. The home team attacks toward the ring on the right.

explain:
Ball sports are also often grouped by style of play. One commonly used classification is as follows.
- **Invasion type**: a style in which teams enter the opponent's territory to score. Ringball is close to this type.
- **Net type**: a style in which the ball is sent over a net that separates the two sides.
- **Striking-fielding type**: a style in which the ball is struck and the batting side runs, while the fielding side retrieves the ball.
The way of classifying these differs slightly among researchers.

When talking about plans for winning a game, **strategy** and **tactics** are often distinguished. Strategy is the broad policy that looks at the whole game or season, while tactics are the specific movements used in the moment against the opponent. Usage can differ slightly from book to book.

In attack, the basic idea is to create and use **space** that the opposing defense finds hard to block; in defense, it is to reduce that space and press the player with the ball. In either case, it is considered advantageous to create a **numerical advantage**, in which one side has more players in a particular area.

The home team needs to create room for a teammate to enter the scoring zone, but the zone is already occupied by an away-team player, so that route is blocked.
In this way, the rules determine where a team can score, and tactics determine how to create space within those rules.

sps-06.title: Sport and Society
explain: Sport is a physical activity and also a **social institution**. Schools, communities, nations, the media, and the economy are all intertwined with it, so there is research that examines sport through a social lens. This lesson does not give one position as the correct answer; instead, it introduces several perspectives in a balanced way.

Let us start with the hopeful aspects. Sport is described as a setting for **socialization**, in which people learn things such as rules, cooperation, and how to accept winning and losing. It is also considered to foster a **sense of community belonging** as people cheer for the same team or region, and to encourage more health-related activity.

There are also concerns. **Win-at-all-costs mindset** is the problem that when only winning matters, fairness and safety can be pushed aside. The **access gap** is the problem that some people find it hard to take part because of factors such as facilities, cost, time, gender, or disability. **Commercialization** is the phenomenon in which broadcasting rights, advertising, and sponsorship affect games and athletes; it is evaluated both as helpful for popularizing a sport and as a concern that it blurs the original purpose of competition.

explain.alt: A diagram with a left box listing the hopeful aspects (health promotion, a sense of community belonging, learning the experience of rules) and a right box listing the concerns (win-at-all-costs mindset, access gaps, excessive commercialization).
explain.caption: Two views of sport

explain: **Fairness** is the core of sport ethics. It is often expressed through the notion of **fair play**, meaning the attitude of following the rules and respecting one's opponent. Acts that break the rules to gain an advantage are seen as violating the basic agreement of competition. **Doping**, the use of prohibited methods to enhance performance, is also a problem in the same context, and fairness and athletes' health are discussed together.

Both the view that sport unites society and the criticism that it instead reproduces existing inequalities are studied. Rather than declaring one side correct, the stance of this discipline is to examine **what evidence supports a claim**.

This single case shows both a hopeful aspect and an access gap. One case cannot support a general conclusion, but it does suggest which questions to ask.

sps-07.title: Energy Metabolic Systems and Exercise Duration
explain: The direct chemical energy that human muscle cells use when they contract and produce force is **adenosine triphosphate** (ATP). However, the amount of pure ATP stored in skeletal muscle is extremely small, enough to sustain only a few maximal contractions (about 1 to 2 seconds). Therefore, to keep exercising, the body must continuously break down stored substrates and resynthesize ATP.

The human body activates three complementary energy supply systems, in sequence and in combination, depending on the intensity and duration of exercise.
1. **ATP-PCr system** (phosphagen system): breaks down the high-energy phosphate bond of phosphocreatine (PCr) stored in muscle to resynthesize ATP from ADP immediately. It needs no oxygen and produces no by-products, and its reaction rate is the fastest, but its capacity is small, so it is depleted after about 5 to 10 seconds of maximal power (e.g., a 100 m sprint or weightlifting).
2. **Glycolysis** (lactic acid system, anaerobic glycolytic system): breaks down glycogen in muscle or blood glucose without oxygen to produce lactate and ATP. It supplies most of the energy during maximal-intensity exercise lasting about 30 seconds to 2 minutes. When hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$) accumulate and the intracellular pH becomes acidic, severe muscle fatigue is induced.
3. **Oxidative system** (aerobic system): uses oxygen within the mitochondria to fully oxidize carbohydrates, fats (through beta-oxidation), and proteins (through the TCA cycle and the electron transport chain). The rate of ATP synthesis is the slowest, but it produces a vast amount of energy and can continue for dozens of hours or more.

The important point is that during exercise no single system works alone at 100%. Instead, the three systems contribute in an overlapping manner along a continuum without sharp breaks. In a 400 m run (about 45 to 50 seconds), the glycolytic system is dominant, but the phosphagen and oxidative systems also contribute at the same time.

Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (**EPOC**, Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption): right after intense exercise, oxygen uptake remains at a higher level than at rest even after the exercise has ended. This is because additional oxygen is consumed to resynthesize the depleted PCr, to re-saturate blood and muscle with oxygen, to resynthesize glycogen from lactate (the Cori cycle), and to maintain the elevated body temperature and heart rate.

Caveat: lactate is not itself the fatigue substance; rather, it is recycled as an excellent oxidative fuel in the heart and in slow-twitch fibers. The main causes of actual acidification and muscle fatigue are the accumulation of free hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$) released by rapid hydrolysis of ATP and the increase in inorganic phosphate ($\text{P}_i$).

examples.title: Analyzing the main energy system for each event
body: Condition: compare a 100 m sprint (about 10 seconds), an 800 m run (about 1 minute 50 seconds), and a marathon (two hours or more).
Step 1: in maximal-power exercise lasting under 10 seconds, the phosphagen (ATP-PCr) system contributes more than 80%.
Step 2: the 800 m is a transition point at which the glycolytic system (about 50 to 60%) and the oxidative system (about 40%) share energy almost equally.
Interpretation: since more than 98% of a marathon depends on the oxidative system, maximizing the rate of fat oxidation to prevent glycogen depletion becomes the key strategy.

Step 1: after 30 seconds of rest, 50% of the depleted amount is restored; after 60 seconds of rest, about 75% is restored; after 3 minutes (180 seconds) of rest, more than about 95% is restored.

Interpretation: this is the physiological basis for needing at least 2 to 3 minutes of incomplete rest between sets in weight training or interval sprints that train maximal power and explosive speed.

sps-08.title: Maximal Oxygen Uptake (VO₂max) and the Fick Equation for Cardiac Output
explain: **Maximal oxygen uptake** ($\text{VO}_2\max$, Maximal Oxygen Uptake) is the maximum capacity per unit of time with which the human body, during intense maximal exercise, takes in oxygen from the air, transports it through the circulatory system to working muscles, and the mitochondria of muscle cells use it to produce energy. It is used as the 'gold standard' indicator of cardiorespiratory endurance and aerobic work capacity.

The physiological governing equation for maximal oxygen uptake is described by the **Fick principle** (Fick Equation):
$$\text{VO}_2 = Q \times (a-\bar{v})\text{O}_2\text{diff}$$
Here, $Q$ is the cardiac output per minute (Cardiac Output, L/min), and $(a-\bar{v})\text{O}_2\text{diff}$ is the arteriovenous oxygen difference (Arteriovenous Oxygen Difference, mL $\text{O}_2$/100 mL blood).

Cardiac output $Q$ is in turn defined as the product of **heart rate** ($\text{HR}$, beats/min) and **stroke volume** ($\text{SV}$, Stroke Volume, mL/beat), the volume of blood the left ventricle ejects in a single beat:
$$Q = \text{HR} \times \text{SV}$$
Therefore, $\text{VO}_2\max$ is determined by two pillars: how vigorously the cardiovascular system pumps oxygenated blood throughout the body (central factor: $Q = \text{HR} \times \text{SV}$), and how efficiently active muscles extract oxygen from the blood delivered through the capillary network and mitochondria (peripheral factor: arteriovenous oxygen difference).

Dramatic adaptations of the circulatory system to endurance training:
- Elite endurance athletes show almost no difference, or even a slightly lower value, in maximal heart rate ($\text{HR}_{\max}$) compared with untrained people.
- The decisive difference arises in **stroke volume ($\text{SV}$)**. The left ventricular volume of the heart expands (eccentric hypertrophy), myocardial contractility is strengthened, and plasma volume increases by 15 to 20% (an increase in end-diastolic volume according to the Frank-Starling law), so stroke volume rises dramatically from 100 to 120 mL before training to 160 to 200 mL or more.
- As a result, the **athletic bradycardia** phenomenon appears, in which resting heart rate drops sharply to below 60 beats per minute (sometimes to around 40).

Units of measurement and body-weight adjustment: absolute $\text{VO}_2\max$ is expressed in $\text{L/min}$ and favors people with greater body mass. However, in sports that move one's own body, such as running or cycling, the relative value per unit of body weight, $\text{mL/kg/min}$, is used as the standard. Typical values are about 35 to 45 for adult men and 30 to 38 for women, while elite marathon runners and cross-country skiers reach 75 to 85 $\text{mL/kg/min}$.

examples.title: Calculating maximal oxygen uptake with the Fick equation
body: Condition: during maximal exercise, an athlete has a heart rate $\text{HR} = 190\text{ bpm}$, a stroke volume $\text{SV} = 150\text{ mL/beat}$, an arterial oxygen content $C_a\text{O}_2 = 20\text{ mL/dL}$, and a mixed venous oxygen content $C_v\text{O}_2 = 4\text{ mL/dL}$.
Step 1: cardiac output $Q = 190 \times 0.150 = 28.5\text{ L/min}$.
Step 2: arteriovenous oxygen difference $(a-\bar{v})\text{O}_2\text{diff} = 20 - 4 = 16\text{ mL/dL} = 160\text{ mL/L} = 0.16\text{ L/L}$.
Step 3: $\text{VO}_2\max = 28.5 \times 0.16 = 4.56\text{ L/min}$.

Interpretation: if the athlete weighs 60 kg, the relative value per unit of body weight is $\text{VO}_2\max = (4560 \div 60) = 76\text{ mL/kg/min}$, which is at the level of world-class endurance athletes.

examples.title: Comparing cardiac output at rest and at maximal exercise
body: Condition: for a person at rest with $\text{HR} = 70\text{ bpm}$ and $\text{SV} = 70\text{ mL}$, cardiac output is $70 \times 70 = 4900\text{ mL/min} \approx 5\text{ L/min}$.

At maximal exercise, when $\text{HR} = 195\text{ bpm}$ and $\text{SV} = 120\text{ mL}$, cardiac output becomes $195 \times 120 = 23400\text{ mL/min} = 23.4\text{ L/min}$, an increase of about 4.7 times.

sps-09.title: Lactate Threshold (LT) and Ventilatory Threshold (VT): Physiology of Endurance Training
explain: Even when two athletes have the same maximal oxygen uptake ($\text{VO}_2\max$), it is often a different athlete who actually crosses the finish line first in a marathon or cycling race. The key to predicting long-duration endurance performance most accurately is the **lactate threshold** (LT, Lactate Threshold) and the **ventilatory threshold** (VT, Ventilatory Threshold).

explain.alt: A curve of blood lactate concentration as exercise intensity increases. At rest it stays around 1 mmol/L, then rises gradually, passing the lactate threshold (LT, about 2 mmol/L) at around 70% intensity; at 85% intensity it reaches the point where blood lactate accumulation begins (OBLA, 4 mmol/L) and rises sharply.

explain:
Let us look at how blood lactate behaves as exercise intensity is gradually increased during a graded exercise test (GXT).
1. **Lactate threshold** (LT): during light exercise, the lactate produced is balanced by its oxidation rate, and blood lactate stays near its baseline (about 1 to 1.5 mmol/L). Then, once exercise intensity exceeds a certain level, the rate of lactate production in muscle exceeds the rate of clearance, and blood lactate concentration begins to rise sharply, more than 1 mmol/L above the resting level. This turning point is the lactate threshold (LT, usually about 2 mmol/L).
2. **Onset of blood lactate accumulation** (**OBLA**, Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation): the point at which exercise intensity rises further and blood lactate concentration reaches 4.0 mmol/L. Beyond this point, reliance on the glycolytic system is maximized and the accumulation of hydrogen ions, the fatigue-causing substance, progresses explosively, so the duration of exercise is sharply shortened.

Physiological link between the lactate threshold and the ventilatory threshold (VT):
Hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$) generated as lactate dissociates are buffered by bicarbonate ions in the blood ($\text{HCO}_3^-$) and converted through carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$) into water and carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$):
$$\text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \leftrightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \leftrightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$
The large additional amount of $\text{CO}_2$ released during this buffering stimulates chemoreceptors in the brainstem, causing minute ventilation (breathing rate and tidal volume, $V_E$) to rise far more steeply and nonlinearly than oxygen uptake. This is called the **first ventilatory threshold** (VT1).

Training adaptation and the rightward shift of the curve (Right-shift):
Systematic aerobic training increases the capillary density of muscle and the number and size of mitochondria by more than twofold, and raises the activity of lipid-breaking enzymes, so the proportion of fat oxidation increases even at the same running speed. As a result, the entire lactate curve shifts to the lower right (Right-shift). The LT that used to appear at 10 km/h before training is delayed to 14 km/h, or to 80 to 85% of $\text{VO}_2\max$, so a much faster pace can be sustained without fatigue.

examples.title: Setting training zones based on lactate threshold pace
body: Condition: a marathon runner has a maximum heart rate of 190 bpm and an LT heart rate of 165 bpm.
Step 1: below the LT (heart rate 140 to 155 bpm) is the Long Slow Distance (LSD) zone, which involves no lactate accumulation and promotes fat metabolism and mitochondrial biogenesis.
Step 2: near the LT (heart rate 163 to 168 bpm) is the tempo run zone, the optimal training intensity for improving lactate buffering capacity and pushing the threshold itself to the right.
Interpretation: the zone above the threshold, that is, OBLA and beyond, is used selectively, through interval training, to stimulate anaerobic tolerance and the upper limit of VO2max.

examples.title: Change in the respiratory exchange ratio (RER) due to bicarbonate buffering
body: At rest, the respiratory exchange ratio ($\text{RER} = \text{VCO}_2 / \text{VO}_2$) is around 0.8. When high-intensity exercise causes lactate to be buffered by bicarbonate and non-metabolic $\text{CO}_2$ release surges, RER rises above 1.0, to 1.10 to 1.15 or higher. This becomes one of the objective termination criteria for a maximal exercise test.

sps-10.title: Levers of the Human Skeletal Muscles and Joint Torque Equilibrium
explain: In sport biomechanics, the human bones function as a rigid **lever**, the joints act as the **fulcrum/axis**, the contractile force of skeletal muscle serves as the **effort**, and the weight of body segments or external resistance acts as the **resistance** (load).

The human skeletal system is classified into three types of levers according to the relative arrangement of the axis, effort, and resistance.
1. **First-class lever** (axis in the middle): the axis ($A$) lies between the effort point ($E$) and the resistance point ($R$). For example, nodding the head: the atlanto-occipital joint is the axis, the contraction of the occipital muscles is the effort, and the weight of the front of the head is the resistance. Depending on the lever ratio, either a force gain or a speed gain can be obtained.
2. **Second-class lever** (resistance in the middle): the resistance point ($R$) lies between the axis ($A$) and the effort point ($E$). For example, standing on tiptoe: the metatarsophalangeal joints of the toes are the axis, the full body weight transmitted to the ankle is the resistance, and the pull of the Achilles tendon from the soleus and gastrocnemius is the effort. The effort arm ($d_E$) is always longer than the resistance arm ($d_R$), so the **mechanical advantage is greater than 1, giving a force gain in which a heavy body weight is lifted with less force**.
3. **Third-class lever** (effort in the middle): the effort point ($E$) lies between the axis ($A$) and the resistance point ($R$). For example, elbow flexion: the elbow joint is the axis, the radial attachment of the biceps brachii is the effort point, and the dumbbell held in the hand is the resistance. **More than 90% of the levers of the human skeletal muscles are third-class levers.**

The mechanical disadvantage and evolutionary advantage of third-class levers:
Because the resistance arm ($d_R$) of a third-class lever is much longer than the effort arm ($d_E$), its mechanical advantage is always less than 1 ($\text{MA} = d_E / d_R < 1$). In other words, to lift a 10 kg dumbbell, the biceps brachii must produce a huge tension, several to more than ten times that load, on the order of tens of kilograms, accepting a 'loss of force'.
Then why did the human body evolve mainly with such inefficient third-class levers? The reason is the **maximization of the range of motion and speed**. Even if the muscle attaches very close to the joint axis and contracts only a little (1 to 2 cm), the far end of the lever, the hand or foot, can move tens of centimeters at very high speed. This is a design optimized for sport movements such as throwing, kicking, and jumping.

Static joint equilibrium and the torque formula:
When a joint is in equilibrium while holding an angle, the sum of clockwise and counterclockwise torques must be zero:
$$\sum \tau = F_M \times d_M - R \times d_R = 0 \implies F_M = \frac{R \times d_R}{d_M}$$
where $F_M$ is the muscle tension, $d_M$ is the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis of the joint to the line of action of the muscle tendon (the moment arm), $R$ is the resistance weight, and $d_R$ is the moment arm of the resistance.

examples.title: Calculating the contractile tension of the biceps brachii (third-class lever)
body: Condition: the distance from the elbow axis to the biceps attachment point is $d_M = 4\text{ cm} = 0.04\text{ m}$. The weight of the dumbbell held in the hand is $R = 100\text{ N}$ (about 10 kg), and the perpendicular distance from the elbow axis to the dumbbell is $d_R = 32\text{ cm} = 0.32\text{ m}$ (the forearm weight is ignored).
Step 1: the resistance torque is $\tau_R = R \times d_R = 100 \times 0.32 = 32\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$.
Step 2: from the equilibrium condition $F_M \times 0.04 = 32$, the muscle tension is $F_M = 32 \div 0.04 = 800\text{ N}$.
Interpretation: to hold a 100 N weight in the hand, the biceps must produce 800 N (about 81.6 kgf), eight times that load.

examples.title: Mechanical advantage of standing on tiptoe (second-class lever)
body: Condition: the distance from the toe joint axis to the center of body weight (the ankle) is $d_R = 10\text{ cm}$, and the distance to the Achilles tendon is $d_E = 20\text{ cm}$.
With a body weight of $W = 600\text{ N}$, the Achilles tendon tension is $F_E = 600 \times (10 \div 20) = 300\text{ N}$, so the body can be lifted with only half of its weight as force.

sps-11.title: Ground Reaction Force (GRF) and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem
explain: When a track runner pushes off the track to run forward, or a basketball player jumps high, the only external force that accelerates the body is the **ground reaction force** (GRF). According to Newton's third law (action-reaction), when the foot pushes the ground backward and downward, the ground pushes the body forward and upward with a force of equal magnitude and opposite direction.

explain.alt: Time-force curve of the vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) during landing. Immediately after contact, around 30 ms, a sharp first peak occurs at several times body weight (passive impact peak); then, through flexion of the knee and ankle, a broad and gentler second peak forms around 100 ms (active muscle contraction peak).

explain:
**Impulse-momentum theorem**:
Integrating Newton's second law ($F = ma = m \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$) gives the relation between impulse and momentum:
$$I = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} F(t) \, dt = \bar{F} \Delta t = \Delta (mv) = m(v_f - v_i)$$
The area under the ground reaction force-time curve is the **impulse** ($I$, Impulse), and this impulse determines the **change in momentum** ($\Delta mv$) of the body's mass.
- Maximizing jump power: to jump higher or accelerate faster, one must maximize the net impulse applied to the body's center of mass during ground contact ($\int [F_{\text{GRF}}(t) - mg] dt$). In other words, a large force ($F$) must be accumulated over a short, efficient contact time ($\Delta t$).

Landing biomechanics and injury-prevention mechanisms:
When falling from a height and landing on the floor, decelerating the momentum just before landing ($mv_i$) to zero ($v_f=0$) requires a total impulse ($I = \Delta mv$) that stays constant as long as the falling height is the same.
$$\Delta mv = \bar{F} \times \Delta t = \text{constant}$$
- Stiff landing: when the knees and hips are barely flexed on landing, the stopping time ($\Delta t$) becomes very short, around 30 ms, so the average impact force ($\bar{F}$) surges to more than 6 to 8 times body weight. This impact is transmitted directly to the cartilage, the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), and the lumbar joints, which can lead to rupture.
- Soft landing: when the ankles, knees, and hips are progressively flexed more deeply (eccentric contraction of the quadriceps and gluteal muscles), the deceleration time on contact ($\Delta t$) is lengthened several-fold to 150 to 250 ms, so the peak impact force is greatly spread out to a safe level.

Vertical jump countermovement and the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC):
A countermovement jump (CMJ), in which one bends the knees and immediately straightens them to jump, can reach a height about 10 to 20% greater than a squat jump, in which one remains in a bent-knee position before jumping. This is because elastic potential energy is stored in the tendon-fascia complex through the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC), and the stretch reflex (muscle spindle activity) is additionally recruited.

examples.title: Reducing average impact force by increasing the landing time
body: Condition: an athlete weighing 70 kg lands on the ground at a speed of $4\text{ m/s}$ after a jump and comes to a complete stop ($v_f = 0$). The total change in momentum is $\Delta p = 70 \times (0 - (-4)) = 280\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.
Step 1: with a stiff landing that stops in $\Delta t = 0.04\text{ s}$ (40 ms), the average impact force is $\bar{F} = 280 \div 0.04 = 7000\text{ N}$ (about 10 times body weight).

Step 2: if the athlete bends the knees to land softly and decelerates over $\Delta t = 0.20\text{ s}$ (200 ms), the average impact force is $\bar{F} = 280 \div 0.20 = 1400\text{ N}$ (about 2 times body weight).

sps-12.title: Moment of Inertia, Conservation of Angular Momentum, and the Optimal Projection Angle
explain:
Human movement consists not only of linear motion but also of numerous rotational movements about the joints as axes. In rotational dynamics, the rotational inertia that corresponds to an object's mass is called the **moment of inertia** (Moment of Inertia, $I$), and it is proportional to the mass $m$ and to the square of the distance $r$ from the rotation axis:
$$I = \sum m_i r_i^2$$
The **angular momentum** (Angular Momentum, $L$), which represents the momentum of a rotating body, is the product of the moment of inertia ($I$) and the angular velocity ($\omega$):
$$L = I \omega$$

**Law of conservation of angular momentum** (Conservation of Angular Momentum):
When a person jumps into the air and the feet leave the ground, the external rotational torque acting on the body ($\sum \tau_{\text{ext}}$) is zero if air resistance is ignored. Therefore, the total angular momentum of the body in the air is always conserved:
$$L = I_1 \omega_1 = I_2 \omega_2 = \text{constant}$$
- Figure skating spins and gymnastic somersaults: when the arms and legs are tucked in close to the trunk, the distance $r$ of the mass distribution from the rotation axis decreases, so the moment of inertia $I$ drops sharply. Because angular momentum $L$ must be conserved, the angular velocity $\omega$ increases explosively, enabling high-speed multiple rotations. Conversely, spreading the arms and legs wide just before landing increases $I$, so the rotational angular velocity $\omega$ decreases sharply and a stable landing becomes possible.

Projectile motion and the optimal angle in sports:
The horizontal distance ($R$) of an object thrown or kicked, such as a shot, a discus, a javelin, or a soccer ball, is determined by the **release velocity** ($v_0$), the **release angle** ($\theta$), and the **release height** ($h_0$).

explain.alt: Diagram comparing projectile trajectories and horizontal distances according to release height. At the same height as the ground (h0=0), 45 degrees gives the maximum distance; but when the release height is above the ground, h0>0 (for example, a shot released from shoulder height of 2 m), the optimal release angle is lower than 45 degrees, at 38 to 42 degrees.

explain:
When the release height is zero ($h_0 = 0$, launched from the ground and landing on the ground), the distance formula is $R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$, so the distance is maximized when $\sin 2\theta$ is largest, at **$45^\circ$**.
However, when an object is thrown from the height of the athlete's shoulder or hand ($h_0 > 0$, about 1.8 to 2.2 m), as in shot put, javelin, and baseball throws, the distance equation is as follows:
$$R = \frac{v_0 \cos\theta}{g} \left( v_0 \sin\theta + \sqrt{v_0^2 \sin^2\theta + 2gh_0} \right)$$
When the release height $h_0 > 0$, the **theoretical optimal projection angle that maximizes distance is always smaller than $45^\circ$** ($\theta_{\text{opt}} < 45^\circ$).
Combined with the characteristics of human muscle mechanics (the shoulder and arm can produce more force and speed when pushing horizontally forward than when pushing vertically), the practical optimal release angle of elite shot putters forms at about **$37^\circ \sim 40^\circ$**, and that of javelin throwers at about **$32^\circ \sim 36^\circ$**.

sps-13.title: Motor Control Information Processing and Hick's Law of Reaction Time
explain:
Before a person takes in a sensory stimulus and responds with an appropriate movement, the brain and central nervous system go through a series of cognitive **information processing stages**. The traditional cognitive-psychological model of motor control divides this into three stages:
1. **Stimulus identification stage**: perceives the form, location, and movement of environmental stimuli received from the eye, ear, and skin sensory receptors, and recognizes patterns.
2. **Response selection stage**: decides which movement to perform in response to the perceived environment (for example, seeing the opponent's spike path and choosing whether to block to the left or dive to dig to the right).
3. **Response programming stage**: in order to execute the selected movement, the motor cortex of the brain organizes the sequence, timing, and magnitude of muscle contractions and sends motor commands down to the spinal cord.

Reaction time (**RT**) and movement time (**MT**):
- Reaction time: the pure central nervous system information-processing time from the moment an unpredictable stimulus is presented until the first muscle contraction of the movement begins.
- Movement time: the pure movement time from the start of the movement until the task is completed.
- Total response time (Response Time) = $\text{RT} + \text{MT}$.

Relationship between the number of choice alternatives and reaction time: **Hick's law** (Hick's Law)
Simple reaction time (one stimulus, one response, for example the gunshot at the start of a 100 m race) is only about 150 to 200 ms. However, as the number of choice alternatives ($N$) increases, the information-processing load of the response selection stage grows, and reaction time increases logarithmically:
$$\text{RT} = a + b \log_2(N)$$
where $a$ is the baseline of simple reaction time, $b$ is the information-processing rate coefficient, and $N$ is the number of equally probable choice alternatives. $\log_2(N)$ represents the amount of information in 'bits' (Bit) units of information theory; each time the number of choices doubles, the information-processing load increases by 1 bit, and RT increases by a fixed amount.

Applications to sport tactics:
- Attacker's strategy: the attacker spreads out the number of attacking options ($N$) that the defender must guard against (for example, in soccer, choosing among a pass, a shot, and a feint), thereby delaying the defender's reaction time under Hick's law and slowing their response.
- Defender's strategy: an excellent player reads the opponent's subtle body movements (kinematic cues, advance cues) in advance through 'anticipation', compressing the number of alternatives $N$ to effectively one, and shortening choice reaction time to the level of simple reaction time.

examples.title: Calculating choice reaction time with Hick's law
body: Condition: for a certain goalkeeper, $a = 200\text{ ms}$ and $b = 100\text{ ms/bit}$.
Step 1: when the penalty kick shot course has two directions (left and right), $N = 2$ and $\log_2(2) = 1\text{ bit}$, so $\text{RT} = 200 + 100(1) = 300\text{ ms}$.
Step 2: when the shot course increases to four directions (upper left, lower left, upper right, lower right), $N = 4$ and $\log_2(4) = 2\text{ bit}$, so $\text{RT} = 200 + 100(2) = 400\text{ ms}$.
Interpretation: when the choices double from two to four, the information increases by 1 bit, and the goalkeeper's reaction time is delayed by 100 ms.

examples.title: The difference between simple and choice reaction time
body: At the start block of a 100 m sprint, responding to the gun is 'simple reaction time (Simple RT)', because there is only one stimulus, the gunshot, and only one action, pushing off the block. By contrast, when a baseball batter decides whether to swing by judging whether a pitch is a fastball or a slider and whether it is inside or outside the strike zone, this is complex 'choice reaction time (Choice RT)'.

sps-14.title: Schmidt's Schema Theory and Open- and Closed-Loop Motor Control
explain: A person can throw a stone of a weight they have never thrown before, or hit a ball of a new size, and respond immediately. If, as behaviorists once argued, the brain stored tens of thousands of separate movement patterns one by one, it would run into the limit of the brain's storage capacity (**storage problem**) and into the **novelty problem**, which cannot explain how a new movement is performed for the first time.

Richard Schmidt proposed the **generalized motor program** (GMP) and **schema theory** to solve this problem.
1. **Generalized motor program** (GMP): an abstract memory representation that controls a particular category of movement (for example, throwing, kicking, or walking). It stores the **invariant features** (the relative timing among the components of the movement, the relative proportions of force, and the order of muscle activation) that do not change when the movement is varied.
2. **Variable parameters**: values adjusted immediately to meet specific environmental demands (overall duration, overall force magnitude, the muscle segments used, and so on). Even with the same throwing GMP, the force parameter is increased when throwing farther, and the muscle parameter is changed when throwing with the left hand.

Two pillars of the schema: the recall schema and the recognition schema
- **Recall schema**: the schema that generates and executes a movement. It forms rules relating the initial conditions of past movements, the parameter settings, and the actual outcomes produced, and uses these rules to determine the motor parameters suited to a new situation.
- **Recognition schema**: the schema that evaluates a movement and detects sensory errors. It accumulates past initial conditions and the results of sensory feedback to form the 'expected sensory feedback' that should be felt when a correct movement is performed. When the sensation actually felt does not match the expected sensation, an error is detected.

Distinguishing open-loop and closed-loop control:
- **Open-loop control**: applied to very fast, explosive movements whose performance time is under about 200 to 300 ms (for example, a golf swing, a baseball bat swing, or a boxing jab). Once the movement has started there is no time to receive feedback and correct it, so the preprogrammed command is carried out to the end.
- **Closed-loop control**: applied to movements that last longer and require accuracy (for example, balancing on a gymnastics beam, aiming in archery, or slowly lifting a cup). During performance, sensory feedback from the eyes, muscle spindles, and vestibular organs is compared in real time with the target reference, and errors are continuously corrected.

Step 1: the shape of the two signatures and the relative time ratios between strokes (invariant features) are remarkably constant (the same GMP).
Step 2: instead of the small muscles of the fingers, large muscles of the shoulder and arm were used, and the overall size and force were increased (variable parameters changed).
Interpretation: the human body does not create a new program each time; it generates an unlimited range of movements by substituting parameters into an existing GMP.

Sensing the instant the ball leaves the fingertips that it has missed, and knowing 'ah, it was short' before it even reaches the rim, is thanks to the 'recognition schema.'

sps-15.title: Practice Design (Contextual Interference) and the Attentional Focus of Feedback
explain: For effective acquisition of motor skills, not only the amount of practice but also the structure of practice and the way the coach delivers feedback are decisive. Cognitive motor-learning research in sport science has identified two powerful principles that overturn traditional coaching wisdom.

explain.alt: Diagram of the three stages of motor learning by Fitts and Posner, shown as a progression. Stage 1, the cognitive stage (what to do? conscious and focused attention, frequent errors, dependence on external feedback); stage 2, the associative stage (how to do it? formation of coordination, reduction of errors); stage 3, the autonomous stage (autonomous execution, spare attention, focus on environmental strategy, autonomous error correction).

explain:
Practice arrangement and the contextual interference effect (**Contextual Interference Effect**):
- **Blocked practice**: a method in which task A is practiced 30 times in a row, then task B 30 times, then task C 30 times, in sequence (for example, hitting 100 forehands in a row and then 100 backhands in tennis).
- **Random practice**: a method in which tasks A, B, and C are shuffled randomly (for example, alternating forehand, volley, and backhand unpredictably, one each).
- **The paradox of contextual interference**: judging only by performance on the day of practice, the blocked-practice group appears to make fewer mistakes and perform well immediately. However, when tested days later in an actual game or a retention test, the random-practice group shows overwhelmingly superior memory retention and transfer to real play. This is because the deep cognitive effort of actively retrieving and reconstructing a new motor program on every trial, erasing the memory of the previous movement (the reconstruction and elaboration hypotheses), promotes long-term plasticity of the brain.

Types of feedback and the **guidance hypothesis**:
- **Intrinsic feedback**: the natural sensory information the performer feels through their own vision, vestibular organs, and muscle and joint proprioceptors.
- **Augmented feedback**: feedback additionally provided by an external coach, video, or measuring instrument. It is divided into **knowledge of results** (KR), which tells whether the outcome was successful or provides measured values, and **knowledge of performance** (KP), which points out the form or mechanical faults of the movement.
- **Guidance hypothesis**: if the coach gives immediate feedback at 100% frequency on every trial, learners come to depend only on external feedback and do not develop the brain's internal ability to detect errors through their own proprioceptive sensations. Therefore, as learning progresses, **faded feedback**, which gradually reduces the feedback frequency, or **bandwidth feedback**, which is given only when performance falls outside an acceptable tolerance, should be applied.

Focus of attention: **the superiority of an external focus**
Gabriele Wulf's research team demonstrated that the direction of attention during feedback cues has a major effect on motor performance.
- **Internal focus**: concentrating on the movement of one's own body parts (for example, 'Do not bend your elbow during the golf swing' or 'Bend your knees to 45 degrees'). It disrupts the automaticity of the body's own motor control and induces antagonistic tension between muscles (the **constrained action hypothesis**).
- **External focus**: concentrating on the outcome the movement produces in the environment, or on an object (for example, 'Throw the club head toward that target' or 'Push firmly into the ground to launch'). It optimally activates the autonomous and unconscious coordination mechanisms of the central nervous system, allowing greater power and consistent accuracy.

When the shooter makes an error that goes beyond 3 cm, the coach provides KP feedback on posture or trigger timing only.

Interpretation: when the athlete is performing well, silence itself becomes positive reinforcement, and it allows the athlete to focus on intrinsic sensations without unnecessary information interference.

sps-16.title: Sport Psychology: The Inverted-U Hypothesis of Arousal and Performance and the Individual Zone of Optimal Functioning (IZOF)
explain: When a player who is normally flawless makes an absurd mistake in an extreme pressure situation, such as the final of the Olympics or a penalty shootout, sport psychology calls this phenomenon **choking under pressure**. Conversely, tension can drain away so much that a player competes listlessly. The effects of arousal and anxiety on competitive performance are a core topic of sport psychology.

**Inverted-U hypothesis** (Yerkes-Dodson law):
If the physiological and psychological arousal level is too low, performance is poor because of drowsiness and a lack of concentration; if arousal is too high, performance collapses because of excessive muscle tension and attentional narrowing (perceptual narrowing). It is a parabolic model in which peak motor performance is displayed only at **a moderate, optimal level of arousal** (optimal arousal).

Movement of the optimal arousal point according to task characteristics and individual differences:
1. **Task complexity and precision**: precision tasks that require fine muscle control and extreme concentration, such as archery, shooting, golf putting, and billiards, have an optimal arousal level toward the low end. In contrast, tasks that use large muscle groups and require explosive power, such as the deadlift, American football tackling, and the 100 m sprint, achieve peak performance at high arousal levels.
2. **Hanin's individual zones of optimal functioning** (**IZOF**):
This model emerged as a criticism of the limitation of the inverted-U hypothesis, which assumes a single, identical middle point of arousal for everyone. The anxiety and arousal levels at which each athlete performs best vary widely. Some athletes perform best in an extremely calm state (a low IZOF), some in a moderately tense state (a middle IZOF), and others in an extremely excited state close to anger and exhilaration (a high IZOF).

Multidimensional anxiety theory and the catastrophe model:
Anxiety is clearly divided into **somatic anxiety** (physical reactions such as an increased heart rate and trembling hands) and **cognitive anxiety** (worry and intrusive thoughts about failure).
According to Hardy's catastrophe model, when cognitive anxiety (worry) is low, physiological arousal changes gently in an inverted-U shape. But when cognitive anxiety is high, the moment physiological arousal crosses a critical threshold, performance does not decline gently; it collapses vertically, as if falling off a cliff (catastrophe).

Cognitive-neurological mechanism of choking:
Under excessive pressure, athletes try to consciously control motor skills that had been automated (**conscious control hypothesis / reinvestment theory**). When a free throw that has been thrown unconsciously for ten years is broken down and consciously controlled by asking 'Is my elbow angle right?', the higher-order motor cortex of the brain interferes with the automated synaptic circuits of the cerebellum and basal ganglia, causing fatal motor stiffness and failure.

examples.title: Comparing optimal arousal levels by sport
body: A national shooting team athlete must keep the heart rate at 60 beats per minute or below and pull the trigger in step with the heartbeat cycle between breaths, so the optimal arousal zone is very low.

A weightlifter in the snatch event roars before gripping the barbell and inhales an ammonia capsule, bursting out maximal power in a high-arousal state that strongly activates the sympathetic nervous system to its limit.

examples.title: The role of routines in preventing choking
body: Before every shot, a golfer always performs an unchanging pre-shot routine: 'look at the target line from behind the ball, take two deep breaths, make one practice swing, and hit the shot 3 seconds after addressing the ball.'
The routine blocks cognitive anxiety (distracting thoughts) about failure and fixes working memory on positive cues only, which prevents conscious reinvestment.

sps-17.title: The Four Sources of Self-Efficacy, Group Cohesion, and Social Loafing
explain: However outstanding an athlete's physical ability is, if they lack the psychological confidence that 'I can handle this situation successfully,' they will collapse at the decisive moment. Albert Bandura defined the belief in one's own ability to successfully complete a particular task as **self-efficacy**.

Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy (sources of information):
1. **Mastery experiences** (past successful experiences): the most powerful and firmest source of self-efficacy. Actual experiences of having successfully completed a similar challenge in the past raise efficacy most solidly.
2. **Vicarious experiences** (observational learning): by watching a teammate of similar ability or conditions perform the task well, one gains the conviction that 'if that person can do it, I can too.'
3. **Verbal persuasion** (social persuasion): sincere encouragement and feedback from trusted coaches, teammates, and mentors, as well as constructive inner self-talk directed at oneself.
4. **Physiological and affective states**: how one interprets the heartbeat, sweating, muscle tension, and nervousness before competition. Efficacy is maintained when these sensations are reinterpreted (cognitive reappraisal) not as signals of fear and anxiety, but as an arousal signal that the body is ready to deliver peak output.

Group dynamics in team sports: **group cohesion**
Carron defined group cohesion as 'a dynamic process in which a group comes together and maintains solidarity in order to pursue its goals or the emotional satisfaction of its members,' and divided it into two dimensions:
- **Task cohesion**: the degree to which members commit and cooperate together to achieve the team's common goals (for example, winning or executing tactics).
- **Social cohesion**: the degree to which teammates like one another and feel personal closeness and a sense of bonding.
In interactive sports (basketball, soccer, volleyball), the higher the task cohesion, the more directly it is linked to the team's win rate. In coaction sports (shooting, bowling, golf), however, excessive social cohesion can actually interfere with concentration on competition.

**Ringelmann effect** and **social loafing**:
In Maximilien Ringelmann's tug-of-war experiment, taking the force of one person pulling as 100%, two people pulling produced 93%, three produced 85%, and when eight people pulled together, the force each person exerted fell sharply to 49%. The phenomenon in which individual members' efforts decrease as the group grows is called the Ringelmann effect.
- Main causes: **anonymity**, in which each player's individual contribution is not clearly measured; **free-rider psychology**, in which one hopes to coast because other teammates will work hard; and **sucker-avoidance psychology** (the sucker effect), in which one thinks that even if they work hard, others will merely go through the motions.
- Solutions: objectively measure each player's activity and contribution (for example, GPS-based sprint distance or the number of defensive participations in soccer) to make it visible, and give each player a unique role that cannot be replaced.

examples.title: A four-step program to boost the self-efficacy of a rehabilitating athlete
body: The strategy a coach applied to a soccer player who feared returning after anterior cruciate ligament surgery:
1. Mastery experiences: start with successful landings from a low 30 cm jump, then gradually raise the height to accumulate success experiences.
2. Vicarious experiences: watch training videos together of a senior teammate who overcame the same injury and successfully returned to the field.
3. Verbal persuasion: the physiotherapist shows objective strength test data (the injured-side strength has recovered to 95%) to instill confidence.
4. Reappraisal of the physical state: the athlete is taught to interpret knee stiffness as a 'natural adaptive response in which the muscle is getting stronger.'

examples.title: How a relay team overcomes social loafing
body: In a 400 m relay team, instead of measuring only the team's total time, the coach analyzed each of the four runners' individual 100 m split times and handoff-zone speeds with ultra-precise video and gave feedback. As each runner's sense of responsibility was maximized, the team's overall time was shortened.

sps-18.title: The FITT-VP Principle and Periodized Training Design
explain: The body adapts to the stress applied to it, but repeating intense exercise without restraint leads to injury and **overtraining syndrome** (Overtraining Syndrome), a chronic state of fatigue. The **FITT-VP principle** of the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM) and the theory of **periodization** established by the Russian scholar Lev Matveyev are the scientific framework for achieving fitness improvement and peaking of performance (Peaking).

The basic components of an exercise prescription: the **FITT-VP principle**
- **Frequency**: number of exercise days per week (e.g., aerobic exercise 3 to 5 times per week, resistance exercise 2 to 3 times per week).
- **Intensity**: the level of the exercise load (e.g., % $\text{VO}_2\max$, % $\text{HR}_{\max}$, % 1RM, RPE (rating of perceived exertion)).
- **Time**: duration of a single exercise session (e.g., 30 to 60 minutes per session).
- **Type**: the kind of exercise (e.g., continuous running, intervals, free-weight training, flexibility work).
- **Volume**: the total exercise workload, calculated as the product of the load, reps, and sets ($V = \text{load} \times \text{reps} \times \text{sets}$).
- **Progression**: the principle of gradually raising the overload in stages as the body adapts (the principles of overload and progression).

Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome (**GAS**, General Adaptation Syndrome) and supercompensation:
When training stress is applied to the body, it first goes through stage 1, the **alarm reaction** (temporary fatigue and reduced capacity). If adequate rest and nutrition are provided, stage 2, the **resistance stage** (recovering from fatigue and reaching a higher fitness level than before, **supercompensation**), follows. If excessive overload continues without recovery, the body falls into stage 3, the **exhaustion stage** (lowered immunity, hormonal imbalance, and chronic performance stagnation).

Temporal hierarchy of periodization:
This is a plan that systematically adjusts the training volume (amount) and intensity so that peak performance (Peak) is reached on the target competition day.
1. **Macrocycle**: the overall training plan, usually in units of one year (four years in the case of the Olympics).
2. **Mesocycle**: blocks lasting several weeks to several months (usually 2 to 6 weeks). These are divided into preparation phases (general preparation followed by specific preparation), competition phases (pre-competition followed by main competition), and transition phases (active rest).
3. **Microcycle**: a daily training program, usually on a one-week basis.
- Classic linear periodization principle: in the early preparation phase, **high volume (training amount) and low intensity** build basic fitness and muscular endurance; as the competition phase approaches, **volume is sharply reduced and intensity is maximized** to raise neural power; and in the 1 to 2 weeks just before competition, **tapering** reduces training volume by 40 to 60% to wash out accumulated fatigue and bring out the peak of supercompensation.

examples.title: Example composition of a four-block linear periodization
body: 1. Anatomical adaptation / hypertrophy phase (4 weeks): 65 to 75% of 1RM, 3 to 4 sets, 10 to 15 reps (high volume, strengthening of connective tissue).
2. Maximal strength phase (4 weeks): 80 to 88% of 1RM, 4 to 5 sets, 4 to 6 reps (moderate volume, high intensity, increased motor unit recruitment).
3. Power and explosive phase (3 weeks): explosive speed training at 30 to 50% of 1RM and plyometrics (low volume, maximal speed).
4. Tapering and competition phase (1 to 2 weeks): intensity is maintained but volume is reduced by 50% to remove fatigue before competing.

examples.title: The Karvonen formula for target heart rate
body: Target heart rate $\text{THR} = \text{HR}_{\text{rest}} + [(\text{HR}_{\max} - \text{HR}_{\text{rest}}) \times \text{target intensity}\%]$.
For a person with a resting heart rate of 60 bpm and a maximum heart rate of 200 bpm, the target heart rate at 70% intensity is $= 60 + [(200 - 60) \times 0.70] = 60 + 98 = 158\text{ bpm}$.

checks.hint: Overtraining is a state of chronic burnout and physiological breakdown.
checks.explanation: Overtraining is a pathological state that brings chronic fatigue, reduced immunity, sleep disturbance, and declining performance; the claim that ability rises tenfold each day is a completely opposite and false statement.

sps-19.title: Capstone: Integrated Sport Science Simulation and Quantitative Data Analysis
explain: In the first stage of the bachelor's capstone, students apply the core theories acquired so far, namely exercise physiology (energy metabolism and the Fick equation), biomechanics (ground reaction force impulse and projectile trajectories), and motor learning (information processing and reaction time), to the experimental data of an elite athlete. They perform multi-step, simultaneous quantitative calculations and verify mechanical plausibility.

Integrated simulation scenario:
Measurement and movement data for an elite multi-event track athlete (body mass $m = 70\text{ kg}$) were collected as follows.
1. **Cardiopulmonary circulation and aerobic capacity test**:
   - At maximal incremental exercise, heart rate $\text{HR}_{\max} = 200\text{ bpm}$, and stroke volume $\text{SV} = 160\text{ mL/beat} = 0.16\text{ L/beat}$.
   - Arterial oxygen content $C_a\text{O}_2 = 20\text{ mL/dL} = 200\text{ mL/L}$, and venous oxygen content $C_v\text{O}_2 = 4\text{ mL/dL} = 40\text{ mL/L}$.
   - Calculation of $\text{VO}_2\max$ via the Fick equation: $Q = 200 \times 0.16 = 32\text{ L/min}$. Arteriovenous oxygen difference $(a-\bar{v})\text{O}_2\text{diff} = 200 - 40 = 160\text{ mL/L} = 0.16\text{ L/L}$.
   - Therefore $\text{VO}_2\max = 32 \times 0.16 = 5.12\text{ L/min}$. The relative value based on the 70 kg body weight is $(5120 \div 70) \approx 73.14\text{ mL/kg/min}$.
2. **Ground reaction force and jump power test**:
   - During a vertical jump, the net vertical impulse recorded on the force plate ($\int [F_{\text{GRF}} - mg] dt$) was $280\text{ N}\cdot\text{s}$.
   - The vertical velocity just before takeoff is $v_y = I_{\text{net}} / m = 280 / 70 = 4.0\text{ m/s}$.
   - According to conservation of mechanical energy ($mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv_y^2$), the center-of-mass jump height is $h = v_y^2 / (2g) = 4.0^2 / (2 \times 9.8) = 16 / 19.6 \approx 0.816\text{ m}(81.6\text{ cm})$.
3. **Projectile mechanics analysis (shot put and discus)**:
   - When an object is pushed out of the hand from a release height at shoulder level ($h_0 = 2.0\text{ m}$), the numerical simulation confirms that maximum distance is formed at an angle lower than the flat-ground theoretical angle of $45^\circ$, namely about $38^\circ \sim 40^\circ$.

Interaction points that a bachelor-level sport scientist must review in the analysis:
- Decomposition of the contributions of the central cardiovascular limit ($Q$) and the peripheral oxygen extraction capacity of the active muscles
- The combined effect of the rate of force development (RFD) of the ground reaction force during jumping and the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC)
- Review of kinematic landing techniques that lengthen the joint loading time during landing to block injury while still exerting high power

examples.title: Multi-step inference of composite physical quantities
body: Step 1 (circulatory system): cardiac output $Q = 200 \times 0.16 = 32\text{ L/min}$, and $\text{VO}_2\max = 32 \times 0.16 = 5.12\text{ L/min}$.
Step 2 (mechanics): net impulse $280\text{ N}\cdot\text{s} \implies v_y = 4.0\text{ m/s} \implies h = 81.6\text{ cm}$.

Step 3 (integrated judgment): this athlete combines world-class aerobic endurance (73 mL/kg/min) with top-level explosive power (a vertical jump of more than 80 cm), making them a top-level multi-capacity athlete.

examples.title: Calculating the SSC efficiency index
body: Comparing the difference between the countermovement jump (CMJ height 81.6 cm) and the squat jump (SJ height 70.0 cm), $\text{EUR}(Elastic Utilization Ratio) = 81.6 / 70.0 \approx 1.165$, demonstrates that about 16.5% additional power is produced through the use of elastic energy.

checks.hint: Recall the elastic energy return of the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) and the stretch reflex mechanism.

sps-20.title: Capstone: Field Prescription and Comprehensive Training Design in Sport Science
explain: In stage 2 of the capstone, the final gateway of the sport science bachelor's program, students set up a hypothetical athlete (or team) in a particular sport, diagnose the technical and physiological faults that the athlete is experiencing, and complete a professional comprehensive sport-science prescription report that integrates biomechanical correction, motor-learning practice design, and periodized training into one plan.

The four core areas of the comprehensive prescription task:
1. **Diagnosis of biomechanical faults and mechanical correction**:
   - Interpret 2D/3D movement analysis data or ground reaction force curves to identify the causes of problems such as inefficient use of levers, wasted moment arms, failed impact absorption (stiff landing), and poor projection angles.
   - Example: diagnose the risk of an ACL rupture caused by knee valgus and a short ground contact time when a volleyball spiker lands, and correct the landing mechanics so that the hips and gluteal muscles absorb the load in a flexed landing.
2. **Design of motor-learning and feedback programs**:
   - Induce the contextual interference effect by arranging random practice.
   - Avoid internal focus (pointing out body parts) and develop external-focus cues (concentrating on the target and the trajectory of the equipment).
   - Apply faded feedback or bandwidth feedback to prevent dependence on the guidance hypothesis.
3. **FITT-VP and periodized training prescription**:
   - Set one-year macrocycle goals and a tapering plan timed to the competition day.
   - Coordinate volume and intensity by stage: preparation phase (hypertrophy and anatomical adaptation), then maximal strength phase, then power and transition phases.
   - Place tempo runs and interval programs that improve the lactate threshold (LT) and improve cardiac output based on the Fick equation.
4. **Sport psychology support and mental routines**:
   - Regulate arousal through exploration of the individual zone of optimal functioning (IZOF) (breathing relaxation and positive self-talk).
   - Establish an unchanging pre-shot or pre-performance routine to prevent choking, and reinforce the four sources of self-efficacy (accumulating mastery experiences).

Through this task, learners go beyond memorizing the knowledge of a single discipline and demonstrate the practical problem-solving competence of a professional sport scientist, one who organically connects an athlete's biomechanics, physiology, and psychology to bring about real improvement in performance and the prevention of injury.

examples.title: Summary of a jump-landing biomechanics and training-improvement prescription for a volleyball player
body: Diagnosis: at landing, the first peak of the vertical ground reaction force is excessive at 7.5 times body weight, and the knee collapses inward (excessive knee valgus moment).
Mechanical correction: introduce hip-hinge and gluteus medius eccentric strengthening training to lengthen the landing deceleration time from 40 ms to 180 ms.
Motor learning: instead of 'Do not straighten your knees' (internal focus), apply the cue 'Land so softly that your feet make no sound, pressing the floor as lightly as a feather' (external focus).
Periodization: after four weeks of plyometric training with progressively decreasing volume before the season, carry out a 50% volume taper 10 days before the competition.

examples.title: Summary of a lactate-threshold rightward-shift periodization prescription for a marathon runner
body: Diagnosis: VO₂max is excellent at 75 mL/kg/min, but lactate accumulates early at 14 km/h (the LT is reached early).

Prescription: a 12-week mesocycle with two 30-minute tempo runs per week based on the LT heart rate (165 bpm), and one low-intensity LSD continuous run per week (to increase fat metabolism and mitochondrial capacity).
